result: The manuscript provides background on peptidoglycan (PG) structure, function, and biological importance. PG is described as the essential component of bacterial cell envelopes, comprising glycan chains and peptide stems with unusual amino acids and sugars. It confers cell shape, osmotic resistance, and serves as an antibiotic target.
evaluation: Claims C1-C18 are well-established background knowledge about PG structure and function, supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this work.

result: The manuscript identifies critical limitations in current PG analysis methods. While PG purification is straightforward, structural analysis remains time-consuming and labor-intensive. The field lacks automated tools, standardized methodology, and transparent reporting of search strategies, with MS data analysis remaining largely manual and poorly documented.
evaluation: Claims C19-C25, C92-C94, and C112 collectively establish the motivation for this work by documenting problems in the field. These are supported by literature review and the observation that search strategies are not reported in published work. This represents a valid assessment of the field's limitations.

result: PGFinder is an open-source software tool that automates muropeptide identification through dynamic database creation. The algorithm uses an iterative three-step search strategy: (1) matching observed masses to monomers, (2) building in silico databases of dimers/trimers from matched monomers, (3) searching for modified muropeptides. The tool outputs matched structures with XIC intensities in CSV format.
evaluation: Claims C29-C40, C99-C100, C113, C118, and C141-C147 describe the PGFinder algorithm and implementation. The iterative search strategy is clearly documented with appropriate technical details (10 ppm tolerance, 0.5 min retention time window). The open-source nature, Jupyter Notebook interface, and reproducibility features (conda environment, regression testing) are well-described.

result: Application of PGFinder to E. coli identified 60 PG fragments with unprecedented complexity: glycan chains (4.38%), monomers (63.14%), dimers (29.54%), and trimers (2.94%). The crosslinking index was 15.69%, slightly lower than previously reported (23.1%). Quantification across biological replicates showed high reproducibility (Pearson's r > 0.96), with the search identifying >106 masses matching muropeptide structures.
evaluation: Claims C41-C49, C59-C60, and C96 present the core E. coli analysis results. The identification of 60 fragments is supported by Table 1 and Figure 3. Quantitative metrics (percentages, crosslinking index, correlation coefficients) are clearly stated with appropriate statistical measures. The comparison to previous work (Kühner et al., 2014) provides context for the increased complexity detected.

result: PGFinder identified several previously unreported muropeptides in E. coli, including: (i) fragments from amidase activity (4.55%), (ii) deacetylated GlcNAc residues (0.23%), and (iii) glucosaminidase products (0.12%). All novel structures were confirmed by MS/MS analysis. The deacetylation finding is unexpected as no E. coli PG deacetylase has been identified.
evaluation: Claims C50-C55, C107-C108 describe novel findings in E. coli PG. The identification of previously unreported structures is supported by MS/MS confirmation (Table 1—source data 3). The quantitative abundances are clearly stated. The observation about deacetylation is appropriately contextualized with existing knowledge about E. coli enzymes.

result: The proportion of anhydroMurNAc-containing muropeptides (4.55%) yielded an average glycan chain length of 36.05 disaccharide units. This is higher than an earlier study (5-10 units) but agrees with recent work reporting long glycan chains. The higher proportion of anhydroMurNAc compared to literature (2-3%) likely reflects more comprehensive searching.
evaluation: Claims C56-C58, C110-C111 present calculated structural parameters with appropriate comparisons to literature. The chain length calculation is based on established methods (Glauner, 1988). The reconciliation of discrepancies with previous work through more comprehensive searching is a reasonable interpretation supported by the data.

result: Extended analysis using a complex database of 224 structures identified monomers with unusual amino acids. Only four structures (GM-AEJF, -AEJN, AEJK, -AEJAK, GM-AEJKD) were confirmed by MS/MS, collectively accounting for ~7.5% of the 80 structures identified.
evaluation: Claims C61-C63 describe an extended search with MS/MS validation. The requirement for MS/MS confirmation appropriately addresses the increased risk of false positives with a larger search space. The quantitative result (7.5%) is clearly stated with the caveat that only confirmed structures were retained.

result: Comparative analysis of C. difficile strains R20291 and M7404 using PGFinder showed high reproducibility and identified significant differences. Strain M7404 had significantly lower monomers (p=0.022) and higher dimers (p=0.005) than R20291. Six individual muropeptides showed significant abundance differences, likely reflecting different enzyme substrate specificities.
evaluation: Claims C64-C76 demonstrate PGFinder's application to comparative analysis. The statistical analysis is appropriate (Student's t-test with FDR correction), and results are clearly presented in Figure 4. High reproducibility (correlation shown in Figure 4a) supports data quality. The interpretation of enzyme specificity differences (C75) is reasonable but speculative.

result: Benchmarking against published P. aeruginosa data, PGFinder identified 63 of 71 reported muropeptides. Eight missing identifications were absent from deconvoluted masses, indicating deconvolution as a source of variability. The unbiased search corrected four misidentifications (K vs AG) and identified additional unreported muropeptides.
evaluation: Claims C77-C85 provide validation against independent data (Anderson et al., 2020b). The 63/71 identification rate is good, with the analysis correctly attributing failures to deconvolution rather than the algorithm. The correction of K/AG misidentifications demonstrates the value of unbiased searching and is supported by MS/MS and retention time evidence (C82-C83).

result: PGFinder can be used with the free MaxQuant software for mass deconvolution, making the entire workflow accessible using open-source tools. MaxQuant supports multiple file formats (RAW, WIFF, mzXML), and validation with P. aeruginosa data identified all expected muropeptides.
evaluation: Claims C86-C90 demonstrate compatibility with free software. The successful identification of all expected P. aeruginosa muropeptides using MaxQuant (C89) validates this approach. The discussion of file format compatibility (C87-C88) appropriately addresses practical accessibility concerns.

result: PGFinder uses extracted-ion chromatogram (XIC) quantification, providing high resolution, sensitivity, and reproducibility with a dynamic range of six orders of magnitude. While not providing absolute quantification, the relative quantification is suitable for comparative analyses and overcomes UV detection limitations (detection threshold and co-elution).
evaluation: Claims C101-C104 describe the quantification approach. The high reproducibility is demonstrated by correlation data (C59, C68-C69). The limitation to relative quantification (C103) is appropriately acknowledged. The advantages over UV detection (C104) are valid technical points.

result: PGFinder enables identification of subtle PG modifications and previously undetected structures, with applications for novel PG characterization and comparative analysis of mutants. Current limitations include lack of MS/MS processing, requiring manual validation. The tool represents a first step toward standardized PG analysis.
evaluation: Claims C105-C125 discuss applications, limitations, and future directions. While the demonstrated capabilities support some applications (C119-C121), several claims are speculative (C106, C109, C117, C122). The limitation regarding MS/MS (C115-C116) is appropriately acknowledged. Claims about standardization (C123-C124) are aspirational rather than demonstrated.

result: Previous work by the authors demonstrated that shotgun proteomics tools can be used for automated PG analysis, identifying many novel muropeptides in C. difficile with high throughput using microgram amounts of material.
evaluation: Claims C26-C28 and C95 reference prior work (Bern et al., 2017) that established proof-of-concept for the approach. These are appropriately cited and provide context for the current development of PGFinder.

result: The manuscript describes detailed methods for bacterial culture, PG purification, sample preparation, UHPLC-MS/MS analysis, data processing, and statistical analysis. All datasets are publicly available through GlycoPOST and Figshare repositories.
evaluation: Claims C126-C140 and C148-C149 provide comprehensive methodological details with appropriate citations. The methods are sufficiently detailed for reproduction. Data availability statements (C148-C149) meet open science standards.

result: The lack of automated tools has hampered high-throughput PG analysis and prevented standardization. PGFinder addresses these limitations and can capture unprecedented complexity in PG structure, as demonstrated with E. coli analysis.
evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C30, and C97 frame the problem and solution. The E. coli results (60 fragments vs. previous reports) support the claim of capturing unprecedented complexity. The tool's capabilities address the stated limitations, though widespread adoption for standardization remains to be demonstrated.
